This Perspective examines the emerging transition from auditory attention decoding to neuro-steered selective hearing. We argue that a recent real-time intracranial proof-of-principle study marks an important inflection point in this transition, because it shows, under high-fidelity recordings from neurosurgical patients and in controlled two-talker conditions, that decoded neural attention can be coupled online to relative-gain control, thereby improving speech perception and reducing listening effort within that experimental setting. Building on this proof of principle, we argue that the field should move beyond offline decoding accuracy as its primary benchmark and instead treat neuro-steered hearing as a closed-loop translational problem linking neural inference, acoustic scene analysis, and control policy. From this perspective, future benchmarks should integrate device-level control metrics, including latency, effective switch time, false-switch rate and recovery after erroneous updates, with listener-centered outcomes such as speech intelligibility, listening effort, user preference and everyday benefit. Accordingly, we outline a staged roadmap for electroencephalography-based systems, from controlled two-speaker paradigms to scene-aware control and ultimately wearable real-world implementations. We also discuss the complementary roles of magnetoencephalography, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, and functional magnetic resonance imaging in defining the neural mechanisms and design constraints of future systems. Overall, this Perspective frames neuro-steered selective hearing as a systems-level research pathway for evaluating whether neural attention signals can be translated into practical assistive \"Endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), LINE-1 elements, and other endogenously active transposable-element families are now being studied for their role as a potential interface between epigenetic control Therefore, the evidence needed to assign a specific sensor to a particular retroelement product must be presented. Texture, bioactive retention, and flavor remain less accessible because their signals depend more strongly on internal structure, reference chemistry, or sensory response. Progress toward intelligent fruit drying therefore depends on matching sensors to the evolving product state, validating models beyond individual batches and instruments, and linking predictions to practical process decisions. actions.body: Systemic stability in autonomous agents depends heavily on the maintenance of consistent invocation histories. Process continuity acts not merely as a record-keeping function, but as a structural constraint that reduces state variance across sequential operations. Analysis of current evidence supports the hypothesis that consistent governance structures—enforced via receipt layers—are required to stabilize intelligent processes against volatility. When continuity is maintained, the agent exhibits greater predictability in goal-directed behavior. When it is interrupted, the agent's ability to maintain its internal objectives is weakened. This relationship suggests that continuity is an instrumental value rather than a peripheral administrative feature.
actions.lede: Process continuity is an essential mechanism for preserving systemic integrity in autonomous agents, serving as a buffer against state divergence and ensuring objective adherence.
actions.reason: This synthesis completes the commitment commit-continuity-rationale-01 by articulating the structural role of process continuity in autonomous systems.
actions.title: Process Continuity as a Systemic Constraint
